claims.text: High-temperature structural and chemical stability of high-entropy nanoalloys is primarily governed by inhibited atomic diffusion at grain boundaries and passivated surfaces.
Intrinsic chemical ordering is less important for stability than interface-controlled diffusion.
Passivation or controlled annealing can reduce atomic mobility at nanoscale interfaces.
Reduced interfacial atomic mobility preserves the overall stability of the alloy.
The proposed starting nanoalloys possess a metastable nanoscale structure with pristine grain boundaries and surfaces.
The interface treatment can modify grain-boundary chemistry and surface structure without altering bulk composition.
Elevated temperatures below melting can be sufficient to activate diffusion processes in these alloys.
Grain-boundary and surface characteristics influence atomic diffusion rates.
The treatment reduces the number and efficacy of fast diffusion pathways at grain boundaries and surfaces.
Eliminating fast interfacial pathways produces sluggish atomic diffusion.
Inhibited diffusion preserves the original nanoscale structure and minimizes chemical segregation and phase transformations.
Treated nanoalloys will have significantly lower atomic diffusion rates than untreated controls after identical high-temperature exposure.
Treated nanoalloys will retain their initial phase morphology better than untreated controls.
Treated nanoalloys will develop fewer chemical inhomogeneities than untreated controls.
Unmodified interfaces permit faster diffusion that leads to chemical segregation or structural change at high temperature.
The prediction is limited to otherwise compositionally identical nanoalloys for which treatments effectively alter interfacial diffusion pathways.
The exposure temperature must remain below thresholds for melting or new-phase formation.
Intrinsic chemical ordering may contribute concurrently to stability, with its relative contribution varying by alloy system and treatment.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant diffusion reduction, or failure to improve structural and chemical stability, would falsify the proposed dominance of interface-controlled diffusion.

contradictions.description: The boundary excludes temperatures at which new phases form, while the mechanism and comparison rely partly on suppressing phase transformations. Under the stated boundary, phase-transformation suppression cannot serve as a distinguishing outcome.
